subject: Medicine
summary: Severe malaria, usually caused by Plasmodium falciparum, is a life‑threatening infection with organ dysfunction. Prompt recognition, rapid parasitic clearance and supportive care are essential to prevent death.

sections.p: Severe malaria is P. falciparum infection with any WHO-defined severity criterion, confirmed by microscopy or rapid test.
b: Parasitaemia >5% (or any level with organ dysfunction)

t.b: Confirms species and parasite density; high density supports severe disease
Detects P. falciparum antigen when microscopy unavailable; positive test plus clinical criteria = severe malaria

sections.p: WHO uses organ‑specific criteria; each counts as severe regardless of parasite count.
In endemic regions, P. falciparum is the overwhelming cause; co‑infection or comorbidity can worsen severity.
b: Co‑infection with HIV or bacterial sepsis

sections.p: Patients may have fever, chills, and rapidly develop organ dysfunction.
Targeted tests identify parasite load, organ injury and guide supportive care.
b: Full blood count, renal and liver panels, glucose, lactate, blood gases

t.b: Detects hypoglycaemia or hyperglycaemia; treat low glucose immediately
Assesses renal failure; need for dialysis or fluid adjustment
Shows tissue hypoxia; >2 mmol/L indicates severe metabolic acidosis
Identifies severe anemia; transfuse if <5 g/dL or symptomatic
Looks for pulmonary oedema or ARDS; guides fluid strategy

sections.p: Complications develop quickly and are often fatal without intensive care.
Rapid parasite clearance with IV artesunate, plus organ‑supportive measures.
b: Switch to oral ACT after able to tolerate oral meds
Correct hypoglycaemia with dextrose, monitor glucose every 1‑2 h
Fluid resuscitation cautiously; avoid overload in renal failure
Blood transfusion for Hb <5 g/dL or symptomatic anemia
Treat seizures with benzodiazepines; consider antiepileptics
Broad‑spectrum antibiotics if bacterial sepsis cannot be excluded

sections.p: After discharge, ensure full ACT course, monitor for recrudescence and educate on preventive measures.
b: Repeat smear or RDT 48 h after treatment to confirm clearance
Educate on insecticide‑treated nets, indoor residual spraying, chemoprophylaxis for travelers

sections.p: Conditions that mimic severe malaria’s systemic picture.
Laboratory values may be falsely reassuring.
b: Parasitaemia may be low in early severe disease; rely on clinical criteria
Glucose can normalize after dextrose bolus, masking recurrent hypoglycaemia
Creatinine may lag behind renal injury in dehydration

whenToSeekHelp: Dark urine with rapid decline in urine output

faq.q: Why is IV artesunate preferred over quinine?
faq.a: Artesunate clears parasites faster, reduces mortality, and has fewer cardiac and hypoglycaemic side‑effects.

faq.q: Can a patient with low parasite count still have severe malaria?
faq.a: Yes; any WHO severity criterion (e.g., cerebral involvement) makes it severe regardless of count.

faq.q: What is the role of antibiotics in severe malaria?
faq.a: Give broad‑spectrum antibiotics until bacterial sepsis is ruled out, because co‑infection is common in low‑resource settings.

exam: List the WHO criteria that define severe malaria and explain why each indicates organ dysfunction.
Describe the first‑line antimalarial regimen for severe P. falciparum infection and the rationale for switching to oral therapy.
Identify three red‑flag complications of severe malaria and the immediate management steps for each.
